<description>
{
 "summary": "Copies the base JSONRPCRequest into a fresh local instance for each element in a JSON-RPC batch instead of parsing every element into a shared instance. This ensures that parsing errors on non-object elements do not inherit the ID, version, or notification status of the preceding element.",
 "problem": "When processing a JSON-RPC batch, ExecuteHTTPRPC reuses a single JSONRPCRequest across all elements. If a batch element is not a JSON object, parse() throws an exception before updating request metadata, causing the resulting error reply to duplicate the prior element's ID or be dropped completely if the prior element was a JSON-RPC 2.0 notification.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"For `[{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"method\":\"getblockcount\",\"id\":\"X\"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `\"id\":\"X\"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped.\"",
  "Functional test additions in test/functional/interface_rpc.py demonstrate that master duplicates previous IDs on non-object batch elements and fails to return an error when preceded by a notification."
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
